paragraphs: Friend, look at what one man with one ram's horn can do. Sheba blows it, shouts, and "all the men of Israel deserted David to follow Sheba son of Bichri" (2 Samuel 20:1-2). The people had just been through Absalom's rebellion, and they were still raw. Hurt and angry hearts are easy to follow a loud voice, and I think that's the warning here: be careful who you follow when everybody's upset.

Now look at the other voice in this story. Joab walks up to Amasa saying, "Are you well, my brother?" while a dagger is already out (2 Samuel 20:9-10). That's a friendly face with a heart that wasn't friendly. Then comes a wise woman in Abel-beth-maacah, and she says, "Why would you swallow up the LORD's inheritance?" (2 Samuel 20:19). Joab's troops were battering the wall, and she asked him to come talk. Joab said he wanted Sheba alone, she took her wise counsel to the people, and they cut off Sheba's head and threw it to Joab. Then Joab blew the ram's horn and his men left the city (2 Samuel 20:15-16, 21-22).

So here's my big idea, baker. Don't just follow the loudest voice or trust the friendliest face. Ask who is really speaking, and what they're really after. Pray for wisdom like that woman had, because wise counsel can change what happens to a whole city. This is the last passage in Absalom's story, and what it shows is a kingdom still broken by people and still needing the Lord's wisdom.
